The Provo Corpus records eye-movement measures and predictability norms for words in short English passages (Luke and Christianson 2018; data source). ## Regression models

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/index/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0fdab1d2bb5100609bf1bd2347a57dc84a69cf6f2671421cbb688d06390a6da8; role: concept -->

The response distribution states which measurements are possible and how they vary; the regression function states how its parameters change across predictor values represented in the data.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A regression model addresses the **response--predictor mapping problem (RPM)**: which parameter of a response distribution should depend on which observed predictors, and through which function? The response distribution states which measurements are possible and how they vary; the regression function states how its parameters change across predictor values represented in the data.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## Linear regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/index/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0fdab1d2bb5100609bf1bd2347a57dc84a69cf6f2671421cbb688d06390a6da8; role: concept -->

Raw word-position summaries and fitted lines remain visible on the same response scale.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The Provo run builds ordinary linear regression in stages. Conditional means state the target, simple linear regression restricts that mean to a line, and the fitting, uncertainty, residual, and diagnostic pages ask what this restriction licenses. Raw word-position summaries and fitted lines remain visible on the same response scale.

## Linear regression

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/index/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0fdab1d2bb5100609bf1bd2347a57dc84a69cf6f2671421cbb688d06390a6da8; role: concept -->

Interactions use MegaOrientation's paired past and future means to define frame-specific differences in orientation shifts; the ordinal fit is deferred until cumulative-logit regression has been introduced.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At the move to multiple regression, the running dataset changes to MALD auditory lexical-decision items. These item rows summarize correct retained trials and cannot recover participant effects. This natural break introduces multiple lexical and acoustic predictors, categorical coding, correlated predictors, regularization, influence, heteroscedasticity, and distributional regression without changing data on every page. Interactions use MegaOrientation's paired past and future means to define frame-specific differences in orientation shifts; the ordinal fit is deferred until cumulative-logit regression has been introduced.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## Generalized response distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/index/08-concept; notes-page: regression-models/index.qmd; note-sha256: 0fdab1d2bb5100609bf1bd2347a57dc84a69cf6f2671421cbb688d06390a6da8; role: concept -->

Generalized linear models retain a predictor-dependent parameter while changing the response family and link.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A Gaussian straight-line mean is not appropriate for every linguistic response. Binary choices, ordinal judgments, counts, and bounded sliders have different supports and patterns of variation. Generalized linear models retain a predictor-dependent parameter while changing the response family and link.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## Conditional means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/regression-models/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/regression-models.qmd; note-sha256: cadffe15ff36f151c177b120b1967f26b3259d72e964621971d4e535137c70ea; role: math -->

Regression begins by naming a response distribution at each predictor value. Its first target is usually the **conditional mean function**

$$
m(x)\equiv\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
$$

m(x)\equiv\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
$$

## The Provo Regression Sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/regression-models/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/regression-models.qmd; note-sha256: cadffe15ff36f151c177b120b1967f26b3259d72e964621971d4e535137c70ea; role: concept -->

It is not a participant trial.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We develop this idea with the **Provo Regression Sequence (PRS)**. Luke and Christianson (2018) collected cloze norms and eye movements for 55 English passages; the Provo OSF release is available under CC BY 4.0. The course table retains complete content-word positions. A row is a word position nested in a passage after first-fixation durations have been aggregated across readers. It is not a participant trial.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## The Provo Regression Sequence {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/regression-models/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/regression-models.qmd; note-sha256: cadffe15ff36f151c177b120b1967f26b3259d72e964621971d4e535137c70ea; role: math -->

The release variable `OrthoMatchModel` is a fitted cloze probability that avoids exact zero and one. It is not a language-model probability. We call

$$
X_i=-\log_2(\widehat p_i)
$$

**modeled cloze surprisal**, and let $Y_i$ be the mean log first-fixation duration at position $i$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## Estimating a changing center {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/regression-models/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/regression-models.qmd; note-sha256: cadffe15ff36f151c177b120b1967f26b3259d72e964621971d4e535137c70ea; role: math -->

Exact predictor values are nearly continuous, so an empirical conditional mean at one exact value would usually contain few observations. Equal-count bins provide a descriptive estimate:

$$
\widehat m_b
\equiv
\frac{1}{n_b}\sum_{i:X_i\in B_b}Y_i,
$$

where $B_b$ is surprisal bin $b$ and $n_b$ is its observed number of positions.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## Fitting the PRS line {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/simple-linear-regression/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/simple-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 0d4cc77fe7880eaf2bcf5de23f97abd74e3e750c587f46f9095594e69dac4b50; role: math -->

The slope is a contrast between conditional means:

$$
m(x+1)-m(x)
=
\{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)\}
-\{\beta_0+\beta_1x\}
=\beta_1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The slope is a contrast between conditional means:

$$
m(x+1)-m(x)
=
\{\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)\}
-\{\beta_0+\beta_1x\}
=\beta_1.
$$

## Centering a predictor

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/centering-predictors/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 98b5a33a10d6c0ca8dd3729b061430a5407d8327e6f4150a8083437ff6edf567; role: concept -->

**Centering** changes that reference value while preserving all fitted comparisons.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The intercept of a regression is the fitted conditional mean where every predictor equals zero. **Centering** changes that reference value while preserving all fitted comparisons.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd
:::

## Reparameterizing the PRS {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/centering-predictors/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 98b5a33a10d6c0ca8dd3729b061430a5407d8327e6f4150a8083437ff6edf567; role: math -->

Let $X_i$ be modeled cloze surprisal and let $c$ be its observed sample mean. Define

$$
X_i^c=X_i-c.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $X_i$ be modeled cloze surprisal and let $c$ be its observed sample mean. Define

$$
X_i^c=X_i-c.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd
:::

## Reparameterizing the PRS {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/centering-predictors/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 98b5a33a10d6c0ca8dd3729b061430a5407d8327e6f4150a8083437ff6edf567; role: math -->

The uncentered line can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
m(X_i)
&=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i\\
&=\beta_0+\beta_1(X_i^c+c)\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1c)+\beta_1X_i^c.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The uncentered line can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
m(X_i)
&=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i\\
&=\beta_0+\beta_1(X_i^c+c)\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1c)+\beta_1X_i^c.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd
:::

## Reparameterizing the PRS

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/centering-predictors/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 98b5a33a10d6c0ca8dd3729b061430a5407d8327e6f4150a8083437ff6edf567; role: concept -->

It leaves the slope and every fitted value unchanged.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus centering changes the intercept from $\beta_0$ to $\beta_0+\beta_1c$. It leaves the slope and every fitted value unchanged.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd
:::

## Reparameterizing the PRS

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/centering-predictors/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/centering-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 98b5a33a10d6c0ca8dd3729b061430a5407d8327e6f4150a8083437ff6edf567; role: concept -->

The two slopes differ by only 8.7e-18, and the largest fitted-value difference is 2.7e-15.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The observed center is 4.791 bits. After centering, the intercept is 5.2950, the fitted mean at that observed predictor average. The two slopes differ by only 8.7e-18, and the largest fitted-value difference is 2.7e-15.

## Transforming a response {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/response-transformations/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/response-transformations.qmd; note-sha256: 94b3652ceee28193fbd75fe944bbd141a1b0675d376c36a8bd07453cd9800a86; role: math -->

The PRS response is a mean of log first-fixation durations. A **response transformation** changes the scale on which the model treats effects as additive. For a positive duration $T$,

$$
Y=\log T
$$

turns a multiplicative change in milliseconds into an additive change on the log scale.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The PRS response is a mean of log first-fixation durations. A **response transformation** changes the scale on which the model treats effects as additive. For a positive duration $T$,

$$
Y=\log T
$$

turns a multiplicative change in milliseconds into an additive change on the log scale.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/response-transformations.qmd
:::

## What the prepared response means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/response-transformations/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/response-transformations.qmd; note-sha256: 94b3652ceee28193fbd75fe944bbd141a1b0675d376c36a8bd07453cd9800a86; role: math -->

For position $i$, the course table stores a reader-aggregated mean log duration, $\overline{\log T}_i$. Exponentiating it gives

$$
G_i
=
\exp\!\left(\overline{\log T}_i\right),
$$

the geometric mean duration among the retained reader measurements for that position.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For position $i$, the course table stores a reader-aggregated mean log duration, $\overline{\log T}_i$. Exponentiating it gives

$$
G_i
=
\exp\!\left(\overline{\log T}_i\right),
$$

the geometric mean duration among the retained reader measurements for that position.

## What the prepared response means {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/response-transformations/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/response-transformations.qmd; note-sha256: 94b3652ceee28193fbd75fe944bbd141a1b0675d376c36a8bd07453cd9800a86; role: math -->

Under the working model for the stored position summaries

$$
Y_i\mid x_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma^2),
$$

two summaries of the back-transformed position response differ:

$$
\operatorname{Median}(T_i\mid x_i)=\exp(\mu_i)
$$

but

$$
\mathbb{E}[T_i\mid x_i]=\exp(\mu_i+\sigma^2/2).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

but

## From discrepancies to an objective {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/frequentist-linear-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/frequentist-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 262d7b0f994f0af959c8ac3db0fb482397a2058a92d923b7c3db773b09d5c6c0; role: math -->

The OLS objective is

$$
\operatorname{SSE}(\beta_0,\beta_1)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\right)^2.
$$

## From discrepancies to an objective {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/frequentist-linear-regression/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/frequentist-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 262d7b0f994f0af959c8ac3db0fb482397a2058a92d923b7c3db773b09d5c6c0; role: math -->

Differentiating with respect to the coefficients and setting both derivatives to zero gives

$$
\widehat\beta_1

$$

and

$$
\widehat\beta_0=\overline y-\widehat\beta_1\overline x.
$$

::: {.notes}

## Computing the PRS estimate {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/frequentist-linear-regression/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/frequentist-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 262d7b0f994f0af959c8ac3db0fb482397a2058a92d923b7c3db773b09d5c6c0; role: math -->

If

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2),
$$

then the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
=
-n\log\sigma
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2
+C.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If

$$
Y_i\mid x_i,\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2),
$$

then the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma)
=
-n\log\sigma
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2
+C.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/frequentist-linear-regression.qmd
:::

OLS and Gaussian maximum likelihood thus select the same coefficient estimates.

::: {.notes}

For fixed $\sigma$, maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing SSE. OLS and Gaussian maximum likelihood thus select the same coefficient estimates.

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y.

Because a linear transformation of a normal vector is normal,

$$

=
\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

## The coefficient of determination

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coefficient-of-determination/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/coefficient-of-determination.qmd; note-sha256: 46025fff7c0a428fb8bbd4f834cc3b522bc5416d6dfb406cf78fbf7dfa7eba7f; role: concept -->

The **coefficient of determination**, $R^2$, compares that error with the error from predicting every Provo position by the same sample mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The OLS line minimizes squared error. The **coefficient of determination**, $R^2$, compares that error with the error from predicting every Provo position by the same sample mean.

## Two sums of squares {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coefficient-of-determination/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/coefficient-of-determination.qmd; note-sha256: 46025fff7c0a428fb8bbd4f834cc3b522bc5416d6dfb406cf78fbf7dfa7eba7f; role: math -->

The total sum of squares is

$$
\operatorname{SST}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\overline y)^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The total sum of squares is

$$
\operatorname{SST}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\overline y)^2.
$$

The fitted model leaves the error sum of squares

$$
\operatorname{SSE}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.
$$

## Computing $R^2$ for the PRS

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coefficient-of-determination/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/coefficient-of-determination.qmd; note-sha256: 46025fff7c0a428fb8bbd4f834cc3b522bc5416d6dfb406cf78fbf7dfa7eba7f; role: concept -->

It includes lexical, contextual, passage, reader-aggregation, and functional-form variation that this one-predictor line does not represent.

The straight line reduces squared error by 5.56 percent relative to the mean-only predictor for these retained position summaries. The remaining proportion, 94.44 percent, is not automatically measurement error. ## Computing $R^2$ for the PRS {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coefficient-of-determination/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/coefficient-of-determination.qmd; note-sha256: 46025fff7c0a428fb8bbd4f834cc3b522bc5416d6dfb406cf78fbf7dfa7eba7f; role: math -->

For an OLS model with an intercept,

$$
\operatorname{SST}
=
\operatorname{SSR}+\operatorname{SSE},
$$

where $\operatorname{SSR}=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\overline y)^2$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an OLS model with an intercept,

$$
\operatorname{SST}
=
\operatorname{SSR}+\operatorname{SSE},
$$

where $\operatorname{SSR}=\sum_i(\widehat y_i-\overline y)^2$.

This decomposition yields the equivalent expression

$$
R^2=\frac{\operatorname{SSR}}{\operatorname{SST}}.

## Residuals {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: math -->

The PRS line assigns each word position a fitted conditional mean. A **residual** is the observed response minus that fitted value:

$$
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The PRS line assigns each word position a fitted conditional mean. A **residual** is the observed response minus that fitted value:

$$
e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/residuals.qmd
:::

## Residuals

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: concept -->

It is not the unobserved population error $\varepsilon_i$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A positive residual marks a position above the fitted line; a negative residual marks one below it. The residual is observable after fitting. It is not the unobserved population error $\varepsilon_i$.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/residuals.qmd
:::

## Computing the PRS residuals {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: math -->

With an intercept, the normal equations include

$$
\frac{\partial\operatorname{SSE}}{\partial\beta_0}
=
-2\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

With an intercept, the normal equations include

$$
\frac{\partial\operatorname{SSE}}{\partial\beta_0}
=
-2\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/residuals.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: math -->

At the OLS solution, this gives

$$
\sum_i e_i=0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

At the OLS solution, this gives

$$
\sum_i e_i=0.
$$

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/11-answer; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: answer -->

## Residuals: question 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/12-question; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: question -->

Why must OLS residuals sum to zero when the model has an intercept?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Why must OLS residuals sum to zero when the model has an intercept?

:::

## Residuals: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residuals/13-answer; notes-page: regression-models/residuals.qmd; note-sha256: f056d43b8ed82b16a04845460da1a3f9e66649d688f85b447286443a4b224166; role: answer -->

The intercept normal equation sets the derivative with respect to $\beta_0$ to zero, which requires $\sum_i e_i=0$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The intercept normal equation sets the derivative with respect to $\beta_0$ to zero, which requires $\sum_i e_i=0$.

## The hat matrix {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/leverage-and-influence/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd; note-sha256: 3a94c8f60ebce2158437c37dbe96691db3d98eccbdf0b7c3968fa256c6b624ea; role: math -->

OLS fitted values can be written as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y}
=
\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y
=
\mathbf H\mathbf Y.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

OLS fitted values can be written as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf Y}
=
\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y
=
\mathbf H\mathbf Y.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd
:::

## The hat matrix {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/leverage-and-influence/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd; note-sha256: 3a94c8f60ebce2158437c37dbe96691db3d98eccbdf0b7c3968fa256c6b624ea; role: math -->

The matrix $\mathbf H$ maps observed responses to fitted values. Its diagonal element

$$
h_{ii}
=
\mathbf x_i^\top(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_i
$$

is observation $i$'s leverage.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The matrix $\mathbf H$ maps observed responses to fitted values. Its diagonal element

$$
h_{ii}
=
\mathbf x_i^\top(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf x_i
$$

is observation $i$'s leverage.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd
:::

## The hat matrix {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/leverage-and-influence/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd; note-sha256: 3a94c8f60ebce2158437c37dbe96691db3d98eccbdf0b7c3968fa256c6b624ea; role: math -->

For a simple regression with an intercept,

$$
h_{ii}
=
\frac{1}{n}
+
\frac{(x_i-\overline x)^2}
{\sum_j(x_j-\overline x)^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a simple regression with an intercept,

$$
h_{ii}
=
\frac{1}{n}
+
\frac{(x_i-\overline x)^2}
{\sum_j(x_j-\overline x)^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/leverage-and-influence/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/leverage-and-influence.qmd; note-sha256: 3a94c8f60ebce2158437c37dbe96691db3d98eccbdf0b7c3968fa256c6b624ea; role: concept -->

## Influence

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/influence/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/influence.qmd; note-sha256: 4da8b39bba6964370136b9ba926d87b2945275c69eb4570111fdf86b672444e6; role: concept -->

**Influence** asks how much the fitted result changes when an observation, or a scientifically meaningful group of observations, is removed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Leverage measures unusual predictor position. **Influence** asks how much the fitted result changes when an observation, or a scientifically meaningful group of observations, is removed.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/influence.qmd
:::

## Cook's distance and grouped deletion {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/influence/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/influence.qmd; note-sha256: 4da8b39bba6964370136b9ba926d87b2945275c69eb4570111fdf86b672444e6; role: math -->

For a Gaussian linear model with $p$ coefficients and residual variance estimate $s^2$, Cook's distance for position $i$ is

$$
D_i
=
\frac{e_i^2}{ps^2}
\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a Gaussian linear model with $p$ coefficients and residual variance estimate $s^2$, Cook's distance for position $i$ is

$$
D_i
=
\frac{e_i^2}{ps^2}
\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/influence.qmd
:::

## Cook's distance and grouped deletion

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/influence/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/influence.qmd; note-sha256: 4da8b39bba6964370136b9ba926d87b2945275c69eb4570111fdf86b672444e6; role: concept -->

We also refit after deleting each whole passage.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Large residuals and high leverage can jointly produce a large $D_i$. But the PRS retains passages as a grouping unit, so deleting one position is not the only relevant perturbation. We also refit after deleting each whole passage.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/influence.qmd
:::

This change is computed by removing passage 2, not by inventing a perturbation.

## Influence: answer 1

Residual size measures disagreement with the fitted line, while leverage measures capacity to move it; Cook's distance is large when those features act together.

Residual size measures disagreement with the fitted line, while leverage measures capacity to move it; Cook's distance is large when those features act together.

## Bayesian linear regression {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 82bba2e06a1c79d94a6bb02c58b223017afbc163bc5917d78ef4dbf30a85f5f9; role: math -->

The PRS likelihood can be combined with a prior to produce a posterior distribution over regression lines. The response model remains

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The PRS likelihood can be combined with a prior to produce a posterior distribution over regression lines. The response model remains

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd
:::

## A conjugate teaching bridge {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 82bba2e06a1c79d94a6bb02c58b223017afbc163bc5917d78ef4dbf30a85f5f9; role: math -->

We use the normal--inverse-gamma specification

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf b_0,\sigma^2\mathbf V_0)
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}(a_0,d_0).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use the normal--inverse-gamma specification

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf b_0,\sigma^2\mathbf V_0)
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}(a_0,d_0).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd
:::

## A conjugate teaching bridge {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 82bba2e06a1c79d94a6bb02c58b223017afbc163bc5917d78ef4dbf30a85f5f9; role: math -->

The posterior is again normal--inverse-gamma, with

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathbf b_n
=
\mathbf V_n
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y),
$$

$$
a_n=a_0+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
d_n
=
d_0+\frac12
\left(
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The posterior is again normal--inverse-gamma, with

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathbf b_n
=
\mathbf V_n
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y),
$$

$$
a_n=a_0+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
d_n
=
d_0+\frac12
\left(
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
\right).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression/06-concept; notes-page: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 82bba2e06a1c79d94a6bb02c58b223017afbc163bc5917d78ef4dbf30a85f5f9; role: concept -->

The posterior mean slope is 0.008872, with a central interval from 0.007099 to 0.010686.

## Computing the PRS posterior

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/bayesian-linear-regression/07-concept; notes-page: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 82bba2e06a1c79d94a6bb02c58b223017afbc163bc5917d78ef4dbf30a85f5f9; role: concept -->

It is useful for connecting conjugate algebra to regression, but it is not an independently specified confirmatory prior.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The coefficient-prior location and scale use the observed Provo response and predictor scales. The inverse-gamma shape is one plus the observed design dimension, and its scale sets the prior mean of $\sigma^2$ to the OLS residual variance. We call this the **empirical-prior bridge (EPB)**. It is useful for connecting conjugate algebra to regression, but it is not an independently specified confirmatory prior.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/bayesian-linear-regression.qmd
:::

## Adding predictors

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/multiple-regression/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/multiple-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fa01e69e566ec33ebd7f0667e5571b3ec5803ba807140e2a4872065ef0e66354; role: concept -->

**Multiple regression** lets several observed predictors contribute to the same conditional mean, so each slope becomes a partial comparison.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Simple regression compares conditional means across one predictor. **Multiple regression** lets several observed predictors contribute to the same conditional mean, so each slope becomes a partial comparison.

## The MALD Regression Sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/multiple-regression/04-concept; notes-page: regression-models/multiple-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fa01e69e566ec33ebd7f0667e5571b3ec5803ba807140e2a4872065ef0e66354; role: concept -->

Tucker et al. (2019) describe the Massive Auditory Lexical Decision database and analyze lexical frequency as a predictor of response time.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We now begin the **MALD Regression Sequence (MRS)**. Tucker et al. (2019) describe the Massive Auditory Lexical Decision database and analyze lexical frequency as a predictor of response time. The MALD 1.1 release is available under CC BY-NC 4.0.

## The MALD Regression Sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/multiple-regression/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/multiple-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fa01e69e566ec33ebd7f0667e5571b3ec5803ba807140e2a4872065ef0e66354; role: concept -->

We model mean log auditory lexical-decision time from SUBTLEX frequency, acoustic duration, and phone count.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The course table contains word items summarized over correct retained trials whose response times and frequency satisfy the documented filters. One row is one word item, not one participant response. The table retains the number and dispersion of contributing trials, but it cannot recover participant effects. We model mean log auditory lexical-decision time from SUBTLEX frequency, acoustic duration, and phone count.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1
https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116
:::

## The MALD Regression Sequence {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/multiple-regression/06-math; notes-page: regression-models/multiple-regression.qmd; note-sha256: fa01e69e566ec33ebd7f0667e5571b3ec5803ba807140e2a4872065ef0e66354; role: math -->

The table contains 23756 distinct word items. The conditional mean is

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0
+\beta_fF_i^c
+\beta_dD_i^c
+\beta_pP_i^c,
$$

where $F_i^c$ is centered log SUBTLEX frequency, $D_i^c$ is centered log acoustic duration, and $P_i^c$ is centered phone count.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The table contains 23756 distinct word items. The conditional mean is

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0
+\beta_fF_i^c
+\beta_dD_i^c
+\beta_pP_i^c,
$$

where $F_i^c$ is centered log SUBTLEX frequency, $D_i^c$ is centered log acoustic duration, and $P_i^c$ is centered phone count.

## Design matrices

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/design-matrices/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd; note-sha256: c567ac4ffba39594fe7c70f30799aef0e581c69749c97b6348404715666e569b; role: concept -->

Each row represents one observed MALD item; each column gives that item's multiplier for one coefficient.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A regression formula is converted into a numeric **design matrix**. Each row represents one observed MALD item; each column gives that item's multiplier for one coefficient.

Course note: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd

## From equations to a matrix {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/design-matrices/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd; note-sha256: c567ac4ffba39594fe7c70f30799aef0e581c69749c97b6348404715666e569b; role: math -->

The MRS can be written

$$
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The MRS can be written

$$
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon.
$$

## From equations to a matrix {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/design-matrices/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd; note-sha256: c567ac4ffba39594fe7c70f30799aef0e581c69749c97b6348404715666e569b; role: math -->

For item $i$, the design row is

$$
\mathbf x_i^\top
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & F_i^c & D_i^c & P_i^c
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For item $i$, the design row is

$$
\mathbf x_i^\top
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & F_i^c & D_i^c & P_i^c
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its fitted mean is the inner product

$$
\widehat y_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$

## Inspecting observed rows {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/design-matrices/09-math; notes-page: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd; note-sha256: c567ac4ffba39594fe7c70f30799aef0e581c69749c97b6348404715666e569b; role: math -->

The OLS solution follows by differentiating

$$
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
$$

with respect to $\boldsymbol\beta$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The OLS solution follows by differentiating

$$
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
$$

with respect to $\boldsymbol\beta$.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd
:::

## Inspecting observed rows {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/design-matrices/10-math; notes-page: regression-models/design-matrices.qmd; note-sha256: c567ac4ffba39594fe7c70f30799aef0e581c69749c97b6348404715666e569b; role: math -->

Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations

$$
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y,
$$

and, when $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ is invertible,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations

$$
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y,
$$

and, when $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ is invertible,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

## Coding a categorical predictor

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coding-categorical-predictors/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 0291ab1f54165b95c65e8bd9e7ddf97265e5cbb840761866da721a03a0827bb7; role: concept -->

**Contrast coding** constructs numeric design columns that make declared comparisons estimable.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A categorical predictor has labels rather than intrinsic numerical distances. **Contrast coding** constructs numeric design columns that make declared comparisons estimable.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd
:::

## Treatment coding in MALD

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coding-categorical-predictors/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 0291ab1f54165b95c65e8bd9e7ddf97265e5cbb840761866da721a03a0827bb7; role: concept -->

MALD's part-of-speech field is a word-form summary from SUBTLEX, not a token annotation in sentential context.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We restrict this page to the three largest lexical part-of-speech classes in the MRS: noun, verb, and adjective. MALD's part-of-speech field is a word-form summary from SUBTLEX, not a token annotation in sentential context.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd
:::

## Treatment coding in MALD {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/coding-categorical-predictors/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: 0291ab1f54165b95c65e8bd9e7ddf97265e5cbb840761866da721a03a0827bb7; role: math -->

With noun as the reference, treatment coding uses

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
&V&A\\\hline
\text{noun}&0&0\\
\text{verb}&1&0\\
\text{adjective}&0&1
\end{array}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

With noun as the reference, treatment coding uses

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
&V&A\\\hline
\text{noun}&0&0\\
\text{verb}&1&0\\
\text{adjective}&0&1
\end{array}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/coding-categorical-predictors.qmd
:::

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_VV_i+\beta_AA_i
+\beta_fF_i^c+\beta_dD_i^c+\beta_pP_i^c.
$$

The fitted mean is

\mu_i

+\beta_fF_i^c+\beta_dD_i^c+\beta_pP_i^c.

## Sum coding

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/sum-coding/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd; note-sha256: 612088d360380a7c0281608d33f1587ba75446bc9bfa9e750a7c3bdcf3c4d0fd; role: concept -->

**Sum coding** instead makes the intercept the unweighted mean of the fitted category means at the numeric predictor reference values.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Treatment coding makes one observed category the reference. **Sum coding** instead makes the intercept the unweighted mean of the fitted category means at the numeric predictor reference values.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd
:::

## A different basis for the same MALD means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/sum-coding/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd; note-sha256: 612088d360380a7c0281608d33f1587ba75446bc9bfa9e750a7c3bdcf3c4d0fd; role: math -->

For three levels, R's sum-coding matrix is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr}
&S_1&S_2\\\hline
\text{noun}&1&0\\
\text{verb}&0&1\\
\text{adjective}&-1&-1
\end{array}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For three levels, R's sum-coding matrix is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr}
&S_1&S_2\\\hline
\text{noun}&1&0\\
\text{verb}&0&1\\
\text{adjective}&-1&-1
\end{array}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd
:::

## A different basis for the same MALD means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/sum-coding/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd; note-sha256: 612088d360380a7c0281608d33f1587ba75446bc9bfa9e750a7c3bdcf3c4d0fd; role: math -->

The category-specific fitted means at centered numeric predictors are

$$
\mu_N=\beta_0+\beta_1,
\qquad
\mu_V=\beta_0+\beta_2,
\qquad
\mu_A=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The category-specific fitted means at centered numeric predictors are

$$
\mu_N=\beta_0+\beta_1,
\qquad
\mu_V=\beta_0+\beta_2,
\qquad
\mu_A=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd
:::

## A different basis for the same MALD means {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/sum-coding/05-math; notes-page: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd; note-sha256: 612088d360380a7c0281608d33f1587ba75446bc9bfa9e750a7c3bdcf3c4d0fd; role: math -->

Averaging them gives

$$
\frac{\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A}{3}=\beta_0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Averaging them gives

$$
\frac{\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A}{3}=\beta_0.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/sum-coding.qmd
:::

## Helmert coding

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: concept -->

**Helmert coding** compares each later level with the average of earlier levels.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Some categorical predictors have an order that licenses planned comparisons. **Helmert coding** compares each later level with the average of earlier levels.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd
:::

## Ordered syllable bands in MALD

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: concept -->

The open top band is internally heterogeneous, so these contrasts do not represent equal one-syllable steps.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We group item syllable counts into one, two, three, and four-or-more syllables. The open top band is internally heterogeneous, so these contrasts do not represent equal one-syllable steps.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd
:::

## Ordered syllable bands in MALD {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: math -->

R's Helmert matrix for the observed band order is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrr}
&H_1&H_2&H_3\\\hline % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
1&-1&-1&-1\\
2&1&-1&-1\\
3&0&2&-1\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
4+&0&0&3 % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\end{array}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

R's Helmert matrix for the observed band order is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rrr}
&H_1&H_2&H_3\\\hline % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
1&-1&-1&-1\\
2&1&-1&-1\\
3&0&2&-1\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
4+&0&0&3 % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\end{array}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd
:::

## Ordered syllable bands in MALD

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: concept -->

Because the columns are not divided by their squared lengths, coefficient magnitude depends on this displayed scaling.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The columns compare two versus one, three versus the earlier-band average, and four-or-more versus the earlier-band average. Because the columns are not divided by their squared lengths, coefficient magnitude depends on this displayed scaling.

## Helmert coding: answer 3

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/14-answer; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: answer -->

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/15-question; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: question -->

## Helmert coding: answer 4

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/helmert-coding/16-answer; notes-page: regression-models/helmert-coding.qmd; note-sha256: ecb5db7782eb8f2798c0dcc48dceb74b4c29b7a16ce4ad202a5266eed3fde12d; role: answer -->

Orthogonality is a property of the coding columns; it does not make observed item properties or groups statistically independent.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

No. Orthogonality is a property of the coding columns; it does not make observed item properties or groups statistically independent. The next page reverses the direction of the successive grouping.

[Sources]

-1&-1&-1

## A difference in orientation shifts {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/interactions/07-math; notes-page: regression-models/interactions.qmd; note-sha256: c3b0a3d2180000390851acd0588ba03253f125892d4a52550760dfcdce93d0bc; role: math -->

For frame $f$, define the observed orientation shift

$$
\Delta_f
=
\overline Y_{f,\text{future}}
-
\overline Y_{f,\text{past}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For frame $f$, define the observed orientation shift

$$
\Delta_f
=
\overline Y_{f,\text{future}}
-
\overline Y_{f,\text{past}}.
$$

## A difference in orientation shifts {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/interactions/08-math; notes-page: regression-models/interactions.qmd; note-sha256: c3b0a3d2180000390851acd0588ba03253f125892d4a52550760dfcdce93d0bc; role: math -->

An additive restriction would require the same $\Delta_f$ for every frame. The interaction contrast between frames $f$ and $g$ is the difference in differences

$$
\Delta_f-\Delta_g
=
(\overline Y_{f,\text{future}}-\overline Y_{f,\text{past}})
-
(\overline Y_{g,\text{future}}-\overline Y_{g,\text{past}}).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

-

## Correlated predictors

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/correlated-predictors/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/correlated-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: f4690913518d33104b468ba750c0096015171adbf661e6ad44726602d223c3a0; role: concept -->

**Predictor collinearity** arises when the observed design contains relatively few such comparisons because predictor columns move together.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We now return to the MALD Regression Sequence. A partial coefficient compares items that differ in one predictor while holding the others fixed. **Predictor collinearity** arises when the observed design contains relatively few such comparisons because predictor columns move together.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/correlated-predictors.qmd
:::

## Overlap in the MALD item design

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/correlated-predictors/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/correlated-predictors.qmd; note-sha256: f4690913518d33104b468ba750c0096015171adbf661e6ad44726602d223c3a0; role: concept -->

That empirical relation makes it harder to separate their partial associations with item-mean lexical-decision time.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Longer spoken words tend to contain more phones and syllables. That empirical relation makes it harder to separate their partial associations with item-mean lexical-decision time.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/correlated-predictors.qmd

## Variance inflation from correlated predictors

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/variance-inflation-factors/02-concept; notes-page: regression-models/variance-inflation-factors.qmd; note-sha256: 4b4b4bf8547aed99f0ba8ff5a766c7a7581464a65fcb0993191ec819451f576e; role: concept -->

A **variance inflation factor (VIF)** compares coefficient uncertainty in the observed multivariable design with uncertainty under an orthogonal reference design.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **variance inflation factor (VIF)** compares coefficient uncertainty in the observed multivariable design with uncertainty under an orthogonal reference design.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/variance-inflation-factors.qmd
:::

## Auxiliary regressions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/variance-inflation-factors/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/variance-inflation-factors.qmd; note-sha256: 4b4b4bf8547aed99f0ba8ff5a766c7a7581464a65fcb0993191ec819451f576e; role: math -->

For predictor $X_j$, regress it on all other model predictors and record the auxiliary $R_j^2$. Then

$$
\operatorname{VIF}_j
=
\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For predictor $X_j$, regress it on all other model predictors and record the auxiliary $R_j^2$. Then

$$
\operatorname{VIF}_j
=
\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/variance-inflation-factors.qmd
:::

## Auxiliary regressions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/variance-inflation-factors/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/variance-inflation-factors.qmd; note-sha256: 4b4b4bf8547aed99f0ba8ff5a766c7a7581464a65fcb0993191ec819451f576e; role: math -->

The corresponding standard-error multiplier is

$$
\sqrt{\operatorname{VIF}_j}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The corresponding standard-error multiplier is

$$
\sqrt{\operatorname{VIF}_j}.
$$

As the auxiliary $R_j^2$ approaches one, the design supplies less independent information about coefficient $j$.

::: {.notes}

If the other columns explain none of $X_j$, then $R_j^2=0$ and the multiplier is one. As the auxiliary $R_j^2$ approaches one, the design supplies less independent information about coefficient $j$.

## Shrinking correlated coefficients {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/ridge-regression/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/ridge-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 74b77ce8d6f8d1f10822670d44f538b188b32cfd32d403a38766fda550205142; role: math -->

**Ridge regression** adds a squared-coefficient penalty to the least-squares objective:

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^{\,\text{ridge}}(\lambda)
=
\arg\min_{\beta_0,\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\sum_i
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\right)^2
+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2
\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Ridge regression** adds a squared-coefficient penalty to the least-squares objective:

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^{\,\text{ridge}}(\lambda)
=
\arg\min_{\beta_0,\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\sum_i
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\right)^2
+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2
\right].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/ridge-regression.qmd
:::

When predictors are on different scales, standardization must be estimated from the training data so that the penalty is comparable across columns.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The intercept is left unpenalized. When predictors are on different scales, standardization must be estimated from the training data so that the penalty is comparable across columns.

## Shrinking correlated coefficients: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/ridge-regression/11-answer; notes-page: regression-models/ridge-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 74b77ce8d6f8d1f10822670d44f538b188b32cfd32d403a38766fda550205142; role: answer -->

Full-data standardization uses held-out predictor values to set the penalty scale, so validation no longer evaluates a purely training-fitted new-item procedure and its error estimate may be biased.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Full-data standardization uses held-out predictor values to set the penalty scale, so validation no longer evaluates a purely training-fitted new-item procedure and its error estimate may be biased.

## The MALD phone-count coefficient {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/residualizing-a-predictor/03-math; notes-page: regression-models/residualizing-a-predictor.qmd; note-sha256: 3f784f8639d5a543ff5ccb0c76a69c87bd678bae9ef17934dd0633a0d296129b; role: math -->

First regress phone count on syllable count, log duration, and log frequency:

$$
P_i
=
\alpha_0+\alpha_sS_i+\alpha_dD_i+\alpha_fF_i+R_{Pi}.
$$

Then retain the same controls in the response model:

$$
Y_i
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_pR_{Pi}
+\gamma_sS_i+\gamma_dD_i+\gamma_fF_i+\varepsilon_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

First regress phone count on syllable count, log duration, and log frequency:

$$
P_i
=
\alpha_0+\alpha_sS_i+\alpha_dD_i+\alpha_fF_i+R_{Pi}.
$$

Then retain the same controls in the response model:

$$
Y_i
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_pR_{Pi}
+\gamma_sS_i+\gamma_dD_i+\gamma_fF_i+\varepsilon_i.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/residualizing-a-predictor.qmd

## Changing conditional variance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/heteroscedasticity/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/heteroscedasticity.qmd; note-sha256: aeb61fffcec3554d52d6f229a57c896465ae14214198bf2b0b6e5898c3478a61; role: math -->

Ordinary linear regression assumes one conditional residual variance. **Heteroscedasticity** means that this spread changes across observations:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\sigma_i^2
$$

rather than

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\sigma^2.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Ordinary linear regression assumes one conditional residual variance. **Heteroscedasticity** means that this spread changes across observations:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\sigma_i^2
$$

rather than

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]=\sigma^2.
$$

[Sources]

## Modeling conditional scale {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/distributional-regression/02-math; notes-page: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 18e8bec320c54436c7f9d63c441c623f945e1bc4344ae95099f05464ae1ae1ab; role: math -->

**Distributional regression** gives more than one response-distribution parameter a predictor equation. For MALD correct log response times, we use

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2),
$$

with

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_fF_i^c+\beta_dD_i^c+\beta_pP_i^c
$$

and

$$
\log\sigma_i
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_fF_i^c.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Distributional regression** gives more than one response-distribution parameter a predictor equation. For MALD correct log response times, we use

$$
Y_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2),
$$

with

$$
\mu_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_fF_i^c+\beta_dD_i^c+\beta_pP_i^c
$$

and

$$
\log\sigma_i
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_fF_i^c.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/distributional-regression/03-concept; notes-page: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 18e8bec320c54436c7f9d63c441c623f945e1bc4344ae95099f05464ae1ae1ab; role: concept -->

## A likelihood for grouped item summaries {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/distributional-regression/04-math; notes-page: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 18e8bec320c54436c7f9d63c441c623f945e1bc4344ae95099f05464ae1ae1ab; role: math -->

For item $i$, the table retains only $n_i$, $\overline y_i$, and $s_i^2$. The identity

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(y_{ij}-\mu_i)^2
=
(n_i-1)s_i^2+n_i(\overline y_i-\mu_i)^2
$$

allows the Gaussian likelihood to be evaluated exactly from these sufficient summaries, conditional on the independence approximation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For item $i$, the table retains only $n_i$, $\overline y_i$, and $s_i^2$. The identity.

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(y_{ij}-\mu_i)^2
=
(n_i-1)s_i^2+n_i(\overline y_i-\mu_i)^2
$$

allows the Gaussian likelihood to be evaluated exactly from these sufficient summaries, conditional on the independence approximation.

[Sources]

Course note: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd
:::

## A likelihood for grouped item summaries

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/distributional-regression/05-concept; notes-page: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 18e8bec320c54436c7f9d63c441c623f945e1bc4344ae95099f05464ae1ae1ab; role: concept -->

Greater observed frequency is associated with both a lower item mean and a lower fitted conditional spread in this grouped specification.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The frequency coefficient in the mean equation is -0.0157; the frequency coefficient in the log-scale equation is -0.0082. Thus greater observed frequency is associated with both a lower item mean and a lower fitted conditional spread in this grouped specification.

[Sources]

## A likelihood for grouped item summaries

<!-- generated-slide-id: linear-regression/distributional-regression/09-concept; notes-page: regression-models/distributional-regression.qmd; note-sha256: 18e8bec320c54436c7f9d63c441c623f945e1bc4344ae95099f05464ae1ae1ab; role: concept -->

The model demonstrates separate mean and scale equations; it is not a replacement for the crossed analysis used in the MALD paper.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The likelihood treats retained correct trials as conditionally independent. Because the summaries omit participant identifiers, the fitted scale may combine trial noise with participant heterogeneity and cannot recover participant effects. The model demonstrates separate mean and scale equations; it is not a replacement for the crossed analysis used in the MALD paper.

[Sources]
